pass_a_gloss: First, the name of vow, as far as on my observation I find it placed: when Jacob, fleeing his brother Esau's wrath, [went] to Mesopotamia at Isaac and Rebekah's charges. The wording: 'Jacob vowed a vow, saying: If God is with me...' (Gen 28:20-22 whole). Next, note the name of vow is taken — though in many places different from prayer — for one who with a vow promises to do certain things if he obtains certain things from God; ranked also among customary terms, as in Exodus after the frog plague (2nd of ten): 'Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron...' (Exod 8:8-9). If anyone distrusts that 'pray' is Pharaoh's voice... [gap]. We observed: at gnats (3rd) neither Pharaoh asks nor Moses prays; at dog-fly (4th) 'Pray for me' and Moses 'I will pray... and Moses prayed' (Exod 8:25-30); 5th/6th neither; 7th 'I have sinned... Pray to the Lord' (Exod 9:27-28) and Moses 'spread out his hands' (9:33) — why not 'he prayed' must be examined elsewhere; 8th 'Pray to your God' and 'Moses prayed' (Exod 10:16-18). In many places the name is placed unusually, as Leviticus (vow valuations Lev 27), Nazirite law (Num 6), binding vows (Num 30), Proverbs ([gap] 'a snare...' Prov 20:25), Ecclesiastes ('better not vow...' Eccl 5:3-4), Acts ('four men having a vow' Acts 21:23).
